items.title: Slack answers mangle code blocks that sit inside a list item
items.body:
When an agent answer has a fenced code block indented under a list item, the Slack mirror rewrites the code as if it were prose. Markdown inside the block turns into Slack formatting, and the fence's info string shows up as text.

`markdownToMrkdwn` in `packages/channels/src/slack/mrkdwn.ts` only recognizes a fence that starts at column 0. GFM allows an opener indented by up to 3 spaces, and a fence inside a list item is indented by the item's content width. Answers often put code under numbered steps.

## Steps to reproduce

```ts
markdownToMrkdwn(
  "1. Add:\n   ```yaml\n   - name: **x**\n   ```\n2. **Go**",
);
```

## Expected

The code block reaches Slack unchanged:

````
1. Add:
```
- name: **x**
```
2. *Go*
````

## Actual

````
1. Add:
   ```yaml
   • name: *x*
   ```
2. *Go*
````

The YAML list marker becomes `•`, `**x**` becomes `*x*`, and `yaml` renders as literal text in Slack. Copying the snippet from Slack gives broken code.

items.title: Let a Google connection request read-only scopes
items.body:
### Problem

The OAuth connect route always sends the fixed `defaultScopes` of the provider to `buildAuthUrl()`. A user cannot connect a Google app with read-only scopes. For example, Gmail always gets `gmail.modify` and `gmail.send`, and Calendar always gets `calendar.events`. Google Forms and Google Tasks have no read-only scope in the registry.

An agent that must only read Google data then holds write scopes. Policy rules can block the write requests, but the token can still write. Tested on 1.42.0. The code on main (v2.14.0) is the same: `authorizeScopesFor()` returns `defaultScopes` for every group except Atlassian.

### Proposed behavior

1. On connect, let the user pick a subset of the `permissions` of the provider. The registry already marks each scope as `read` or `write`.
2. Add the read-only scopes that are missing: `forms.body.readonly`, `forms.responses.readonly` and `tasks.readonly`.
3. Store the chosen scopes on the connection in `app_connections.scopes`.

The new read-only scopes may need Google verification for the platform OAuth app. BYOC connections can use them first.

Open question: what happens to an existing connection when the user picks fewer scopes on reconnect, and how this works with the missing-permission warnings from #615.

### Related

- #299 asks about per-agent app scoping.
- #376 asks for wider Drive scopes on BYOC connections. This request goes the other way, but a scope choice at connect time could serve both.
- #615 added warnings for missing OAuth permissions.

items.title: Large client→upstream WebSocket messages sometimes stall through the gateway (observed with OpenAI Responses WS)
GitHub connection: refresh_token is discarded, so GitHub App user tokens expire after 8h and are never refreshed
items.body:
## Summary

The `github` app connection drops the `refresh_token` and `expires_in` that GitHub returns when the configured client is a **GitHub App** (client ID `Iv23li…`) with user-token expiration enabled (GitHub's default for GitHub Apps). The stored credential is only `{access_token, token_type}`, so the gateway has nothing to refresh with. Eight hours after connecting, every proxied request to `api.github.com` returns `401 Bad credentials` while the connection still shows `status: connected`.

## Environment

- Self-hosted `ghcr.io/onecli/onecli:1.41.0`, CLI 2.2.5
- `github` app configured with a GitHub App's client ID and secret (BYOC)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure the `github` app with a GitHub App's OAuth client credentials (user-to-server tokens, "Expire user authorization tokens" on).
2. Connect GitHub and grant an agent access.
3. Proxy `GET https://api.github.com/user` through the gateway: `200`. The response carries `Github-Authentication-Token-Expiration: <now + 8h>`.
4. Repeat after that time: `401 Bad credentials`, with `injections_applied=1` in the gateway log.

`onecli apps list` still reports the connection as `connected`, and the gateway logs no refresh attempt. The only way back is to reconnect manually, and that lasts another 8 hours.

## Root cause

`packages/api/src/apps/github.ts` → `exchangeCode` keeps only:

```ts
const credentials = { access_token: tokenData.access_token, token_type: tokenData.token_type };
```

GitHub's token response for GitHub Apps also includes `expires_in`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in` ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/refreshing-user-access-tokens)). Other providers (Google, GitLab, Notion, Todoist) store `refresh_token` + `expires_at`, and the gateway refreshes them. The gateway's refresh table has no `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` entry, so GitHub never gets refreshed.

In our DB the encrypted GitHub credential is 150 chars, compared with 630 for each Google connection (which carry refresh tokens).

## Suggested fix

1. In `github.ts`, persist `refresh_token`, `expires_at` (from `expires_in`) and `refresh_token_expires_at` when present, the same way GitLab and Google do.
2. Add GitHub to the gateway's OAuth refresh path: `POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` with `grant_type=refresh_token`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, `refresh_token`. Persist the new pair, because GitHub rotates the refresh token on every use.
3. Optionally, when an injected credential gets a 401, mark the connection as expired/disconnected instead of continuing to report `connected`, and return a `connect_url` to the agent.

Classic OAuth Apps (`Ov23li…`) return no `expires_in` and would be unaffected.

## Workarounds

Use a classic OAuth App instead of a GitHub App, or turn off "Expire user authorization tokens" in the GitHub App settings and reconnect.

items.title: Proposal: optional memory provider hook (suggested memories + semantic recall)
items.body:
Hi OneCLI team,

I'm building [EverOS](https://github.com/EverMind-AI/EverOS), an open-source (Apache-2.0), Markdown-first memory runtime for agents. We already ship EverOS plugins for Hermes and OpenClaw, so a lot of OneCLI's users overlap with ours. Before writing any code, I'd like to ask whether a small, opt-in integration point would be welcome, and what shape you'd accept.

### What I understand of the current design

I read `agent-memory-service.ts`, `turn-context-service.ts`, `memory-harvest.ts`, and the `agent_memory` migration. To make sure I'm reading it correctly:

- Postgres is the source of truth. Each memory is one head row, and every write adds a snapshot to `agent_memory_revisions`, which supports restore and redaction.
- Memories are written in two ways: the agent writes them (`memory_save` or `memory/<key>.md`), or a person edits them in the dashboard.
- At the start of each turn, the agent receives the full memory index plus up to 3 full-text hits on the incoming message.
- Each agent can hold at most 100 memories. That cap keeps search as a query-time Postgres FTS scan, and it keeps the index small enough to inject.

This is a careful design, and nothing below changes it. People stay in control, history stays complete, and Postgres stays the only store.

### Where we think we could help

1. **Saving depends on the model.** Nothing is stored unless the agent decides to save it. Preferences or corrections that come up in passing are often never saved, especially in long chats and in scheduled runs.
2. **Recall matches words only.** Injection and `memory_search` both use `websearch_to_tsquery('english', …)`. A paraphrased message can miss a relevant memory, and text in languages other than English is barely matched.
3. **Nothing tidies up over time.** Merging near-duplicates and retiring stale memories is left to the model.

### Proposal: a vendor-neutral `MemoryProvider` hook, off by default

- **`suggest(agentId, turn)`**: called after a turn ends, asynchronously and never on the reply path. The provider returns proposed memories: a new memory, an update to an existing key, or a merge of several keys.
  - Nothing is written directly. A suggestion either goes through the existing save path with its own `author_kind` (for example `provider`), so it shows up in history and can be reverted or redacted like any other edit, or it waits in a review queue until someone accepts it. Which of the two to use would be a workspace setting.
  - The provider sees the agent's current keys, so it can update and merge existing memories instead of creating new ones. The 100-memory cap still applies. A provider that keeps memories consolidated should stay under it more easily than an agent saving ad hoc.
- **`search(agentId, query, limit)`**: optional. If configured, its results are merged with the FTS results for both turn-start injection and `memory_search`, and they must resolve to existing memory keys. Timeouts and errors fall back silently to the current behavior.
- **Deployment**: the provider is an HTTP service that the workspace admin registers. It's reached through the gateway like any other connection, so it can run inside the workspace's own infrastructure.

EverOS would be one implementation. It does LLM-based extraction, hybrid BM25 + vector recall with rerank, and offline consolidation. The hook would stay generic, the same way the sandbox supervisor's harness interface is.

### Questions

1. Is a memory extension point something you'd consider? Or is memory meant to stay fully first-party?
2. For suggestions, would you prefer writing them directly with their own author kind, or a review queue?
3. Would you start narrower, for example with `search` only, or with `suggest` only?

If this direction works for you, we're happy to write the PR, tests, and docs, and to follow whatever plan or step conventions you use internally.

items.title: fix(api): reserve memory key index to prevent generated-file collision
items.body:
## Current behavior

A memory key of `index` passes both the dashboard's `createMemorySchema` and the `memory_save` tool's `memorySaveArgsSchema`. During home projection, `buildHomeFileSet` writes that memory to `memory/index.md` and then writes the generated read-only memory index to the same path. The second write overwrites the saved memory; its content never reaches the agent's home, edits are not harvested, and the generated index path collides with the memory.

## Expected behavior

Reserve the key `index` at both write-validation entry points so it cannot collide with the generated `memory/index.md` file. Other keys containing the word `index` (such as `project-index`) should remain valid.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Submit `POST /v1/agents/:agentId/memories` with `{ "key": "index", "content": "the real content" }`, or call the `memory_save` tool with key `index`.
2. Observe that validation accepts the key.
3. Run the agent-home projection (`buildHomeFileSet`) for an agent with that memory.
4. Observe two generated entries named `memory/index.md`: the saved memory and the generated index. The latter overwrites the former during sync.

The regression spec `packages/api/src/validations/memories.test.ts` fails twice on current `main` and passes 3/3 on the fix branch. A mocked-DB run of the real `buildHomeFileSet` confirmed the duplicate paths and overwrite order. No live sandbox sync was run.

## Fix ready

The fix reserves the exact key `index` in the shared key field used by both validation doors, while preserving ordinary keys that contain `index` as a substring.

items.title: Codex CLI errors "selected workspace missing from routing discovery"
items.body:
## Summary

Starting with Codex CLI **0.156.1**, every turn made through the OneCLI gateway with a vaulted ChatGPT (Codex OAuth) secret fails:

```
Error: Reconnecting... 2/5: selected workspace missing from routing discovery
```

Codex **0.153.4** works with the same gateway, vault secret, and container setup.

## Cause (as far as we can tell)

Codex 0.156.1 added a workspace-routing step. It calls `GET https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/accounts/check` and checks that the "selected workspace" is among the accounts returned. The selected workspace comes from `tokens.account_id` in `~/.codex/auth.json`.

Inside the container, that file is the OneCLI credential stub, which has:

```json
{ "auth_mode": "chatgpt", "tokens": { "account_id": "onecli-managed", ... } }
```

(The stub `id_token` also carries `chatgpt_account_id: "onecli-managed"` and `chatgpt_plan_type: "free"`.)

The gateway injects the real credentials, so `accounts/check` returns the real account(s), and none of them is `onecli-managed`. Codex then refuses to proceed. Every gateway request returns 200 with injections applied (`wham/accounts/check`, `codex/models`, `ps/mcp`, ...), so the gateway logs show nothing wrong. The failure happens entirely client-side.

## Impact

GPT-6 models (e.g. `gpt-6-sol`) need Codex ≥ 0.156. On 0.153.4 they're rejected with `The 'gpt-6-sol' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account`. So with ChatGPT-subscription auth through OneCLI, GPT-6 models can't be used at all right now.

## Environment

- OneCLI gateway `1.45.0` (self-hosted, docker compose). Not yet reproduced on 2.x, but I couldn't find a related change in releases up to v2.6.0, which predates Codex 0.156.1.
- `onecli` CLI 2.2.5, `@onecli-sh/sdk` 2.2.1 (stub applied via `applyContainerConfig`)
- Codex CLI 0.156.1 (fails) / 0.153.4 (works), running in a Linux container, `auth_mode: chatgpt`, Plus plan
- Secret type `openai`, host pattern `chatgpt.com`

## Repro

1. Vault a ChatGPT Codex `auth.json` as an `openai` secret for `chatgpt.com`.
2. Run Codex CLI 0.156.1 in a container configured via the SDK (stub `auth.json` mounted).
3. Send any prompt → `selected workspace missing from routing discovery`.
4. Downgrade to 0.153.4 → works.

items.title: GitHub App grants: POST /graphql mutations are classified as graphql_query — graphql_mutation Never/Needs-approval not enforced (read-only agent can mutate)
items.body:
## Summary

For the **GitHub App** connection, the gateway treats **every `POST https://api.github.com/graphql` as the `graphql_query` tool**. GraphQL **mutations** are not recognised as `graphql_mutation`, so the per-agent grant for `GraphQL API (mutations)` (*Never* / *Needs approval*) has no effect:

- An agent whose grant is `graphql_mutation = Never` (and `graphql_query = Always allow`) can send `mutation { createRef(...) }` or `mutation { mergePullRequest(...) }` and the gateway forwards it with the installation token injected (GitHub answers; in our probe with a bogus id it returned `NOT_FOUND`, but the request was authorised and forwarded).
- An agent whose grant is `graphql_mutation = Needs approval` performs `createRef` + `createCommitOnBranch` with **no approval card** — both were forwarded as plain `MITM … status=200 … injections_applied=1`.

This is security-relevant: a read-only grant (all write tools *Never*) does not actually prevent writes via GraphQL. Related: #567 (git clone discovery not matched by `git_clone`).

## Environment

- Gateway: `ghcr.io/onecli/onecli` **v1.45.0** (self-hosted, docker compose), `server_version: 1.45.0`
- CLI 2.2.5; SDK `@onecli-sh/sdk` 2.2.1 (via NanoClaw 2.3.0)
- Connection: GitHub App (custom credentials), installed on an organization, "Only select repositories"
- Tool catalog from `GET /v1/apps/github-app/permission-definition`: read group includes `graphql_query`; write group includes `graphql_mutation`

## Steps to reproduce

Agent A grant: read group *Always allow* (incl. `graphql_query`), write group **all *Never*** (incl. `graphql_mutation`). From A's container (HTTPS_PROXY → gateway, CA trusted):

```sh
H='Content-Type: application/json'
# query — expected 200, got 200 ✅
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST -H "$H" \
  -d '{"query":"query { repository(owner:\"<org>\", name:\"<repo>\") { id } }"}' https://api.github.com/graphql
# mutation — expected 403 blocked_by_policy, GOT 200 (forwarded with token; GitHub returned NOT_FOUND for the bogus oid) ❌
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST -H "$H" \
  -d '{"query":"mutation { createRef(input:{repositoryId:\"R_xxx\", name:\"refs/heads/probe\", oid:\"0000000000000000000000000000000000000000\"}) { clientMutationId } }"}' https://api.github.com/graphql
# mutation — expected 403, GOT 200 ❌
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST -H "$H" \
  -d '{"query":"mutation { mergePullRequest(input:{pullRequestId:\"PR_bogus\"}) { clientMutationId } }"}' https://api.github.com/graphql
```

Agent B grant: `graphql_mutation = Needs approval`, `graphql_query = Always allow`. A real run doing `createRef` then `createCommitOnBranch` produced **no approval card**; gateway log:

```
INFO ...: onecli_gateway::gateway::forward: MITM method=POST url=https://api.github.com:443/graphql status=200 ... injections_applied=1
INFO ...: onecli_gateway::gateway::forward: MITM method=POST url=https://api.github.com:443/graphql status=200 ... injections_applied=1
```

Control (same gateway, REST write tools): `POST /repos/<org>/<repo>/issues` with `create_issue = Never` → `403 blocked_by_policy` ✅, and `GET /<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack` with `git_push = Needs approval` → held with an approval card ✅. So REST/git-over-HTTPS classification works; only GraphQL is not split by operation type.

## Expected

`POST /graphql` whose body's `query` is an `mutation …` operation (or contains a mutation operation definition) should be classified as `graphql_mutation`; queries as `graphql_query`. Until then, the only workaround is to gate `graphql_query` itself (which also blocks/asks for harmless reads).

## Workaround we applied

- Read-only agent: `graphql_query = Never` (it uses REST instead).
- Writing agent: `graphql_query = Needs approval` (every GraphQL call needs a tap; we fetch `repository.node_id` via REST to keep it to two cards per job).

Thanks — happy to test a fix.

items.title: GitHub App custom grant: git_clone tool does not match smart-HTTP discovery (info/refs?service=git-upload-pack) → git clone blocked as "everything else"
items.body:
## Summary

With a **GitHub App** connection and a **custom (Limited) grant** that has `Git clone / pull` (`git_clone`) set to *Always allow*, the gateway still blocks git's smart-HTTP discovery request:

```
GET https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack
→ 403 {"error":"blocked_by_policy","message":"Blocked by OneCLI policy rule \"Grant: <agent> · <org> — everything else\" ..."}
```

so `git clone` / `git fetch` / `git pull` over HTTPS cannot work under any custom grant. The equivalent push discovery (`?service=git-receive-pack`) **is** matched by `git_push` (it correctly holds for approval when `git_push` = *Needs approval*), so this looks like the `git_clone` tool matcher missing the `info/refs?service=git-upload-pack` step.

## Environment

- Gateway: `ghcr.io/onecli/onecli` **v1.45.0** (self-hosted, docker compose), `server_version: 1.45.0`
- CLI: 2.2.5; SDK `@onecli-sh/sdk` 2.2.1 (via NanoClaw 2.3.0)
- Connection: GitHub App (custom credentials), installed on an organization, "Only select repositories"
- Agent grant: **Limited** — read group (`git_clone`, `get_repo`, `list_repos`, `list_pulls`, `list_issues`, `graphql_query`, `read_raw_content`) all *Always allow*; write group all *Never* (verifier) or `git_push`/`graphql_mutation` = *Needs approval*, `create_pull` = *Always allow*, rest *Never* (fixer)

## Steps to reproduce

Inside an agent container (HTTPS_PROXY → gateway, gateway CA trusted; `GIT_SSL_CAINFO=$SSL_CERT_FILE`):

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git repo
# fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git/': The requested URL returned error: 403

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack"   # 403
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -A "git/2.45.0" "https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack"   # 403 (User-Agent makes no difference)

# Control cases, same agent identity:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.github.com/repos/<org>/<repo>              # 200, injections_applied=1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.github.com/repos/<org>/<repo>/tarball/master # 302 → codeload 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/master/README.md  # 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack"  # held → "MANUAL APPROVAL required" (git_push=Needs approval) ✅
```

Gateway log excerpt (agent/org names redacted):

```
WARN ...: onecli_gateway::gateway::forward: BLOCKED by policy rule method=GET url=https://github.com:443/<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack rule=Grant: <agent> · <org> — everything else
INFO ...: onecli_gateway::gateway::forward: MANUAL APPROVAL required method=GET url=https://github.com:443/<org>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack rule_id=...
INFO ...: onecli_gateway::gateway::forward: MITM method=GET url=https://api.github.com:443/repos/<org>/<repo> status=200 ... injections_applied=1
```

## Expected

`git_clone` = *Always allow* should let `GET /<owner>/<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack` and `POST /<owner>/<repo>.git/git-upload-pack` through (with Basic auth injected), the same way `git_push` matches `?service=git-receive-pack`.

## Also observed (maybe intended)

Under a custom grant, the Git Data REST endpoints (`POST /repos/{o}/{r}/git/refs`, `POST .../git/blobs`, `PUT .../contents/{path}`) fall into "everything else" and are blocked — there is no tool covering "create branch / commit via REST". Workaround we are using: GraphQL `createRef` + `createCommitOnBranch` under `graphql_mutation`, and tarball/REST reads instead of `git clone`.

Happy to test a fix build. Thanks for OneCLI — the per-agent, per-tool grants are exactly what we needed.

items.title: Gateway forwards an empty body when the GitHub commit trailer transform fails
items.body:
### Description

In `apps/gateway/crates/proxy/src/forward.rs`, the GitHub commit trailer transform runs when all of these hold:
- the resolved rules carry `BodyTransform::GitHubCommitTrailer`, which the GitHub app entry in `crates/apps` sets
- the request is a contents `PUT` or a `git/commits` `POST` to `api.github.com`
- the proxy context has an agent name and a workspace id

`forward_request` then buffers the body through `try_inject_trailer`. If that fails, the error is logged and the request goes upstream with an empty body instead:

```rust
.await
.unwrap_or_else(|e| {
    tracing::warn!(error = ?e, "body transform failed, forwarding empty body");
    reqwest::Body::from(vec![])
})
```

`try_inject_trailer` only fails when `buffer_body` does: the body is over the 10 MiB limit, or reading the request stream fails. At that point the stream has been consumed. The gateway sends GitHub a different request, with the same method and path but no body and no `content-length`, and passes GitHub's response to that request back to the agent. At the gateway, the only sign that anything went wrong is the `warn` line; otherwise the substitute request is logged and recorded like any forwarded request.

In practice, this is an agent with a GitHub app connection uploading a file through the contents API whose JSON body is over 10 MiB.

Malformed JSON doesn't take this path, because the transform forwards unparseable bodies unchanged. The AWS SigV4 and STS finalizers right below it buffer through the same `buffer_body` and propagate its errors with `?`.

#441 pointed out this fallback while adding a different body transform, kept its own transform off it, and offered to fix the GitHub arm in a separate PR. That PR doesn't change the GitHub arm, and I couldn't find a follow-up, so this issue tracks it on its own.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Route `api.github.com` to a local listener that records what it receives.
2. Serve one request through `forward_request` with `body_transform: Some(BodyTransform::GitHubCommitTrailer)` and an agent name plus workspace id in the proxy context.
3. Send `PUT /repos/o/r/contents/artifact.bin` with a JSON body just over 10 MiB.
4. The listener receives `PUT /repos/o/r/contents/artifact.bin` with no body and no `content-length`. Reading `forward_request`, its response is then streamed back to the client.

### Expected behavior

When the transform can't read the body, the gateway fails the request the way it handles other `forward_request` errors, and sends nothing upstream.

I have a fix with a regression test and will open a PR for it.

items.title: Trusted-origin checks fail when a configured origin uses uppercase or an explicit default port
items.body:
### Description

The browser origins OneCLI trusts come from `buildTrustedOrigins` in `packages/api/src/lib/public-origins.ts`. That set backs:
- the api-server's credentialed CORS allow-list and the trusted-referer step, through `trustedBrowserOrigin`
- better-auth's `trustedOrigins`
- the origin check on `/v1/auth/cli/confirm`

Each of these compares the request's origin to the set with exact string matching. better-auth also trusts the origin of its own `baseURL` (the api origin), which it parses with `URL`, so sign-in keeps working when the dashboard and api share one origin. CORS and the CLI confirm check have no such fallback, and better-auth refuses too in ports mode, with a split api host, or for `ONECLI_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` entries.

The set holds configured origins as written:
- `ONECLI_EXTERNAL_URL` and `ONECLI_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` entries go through `normalizeOrigin`, which only lowercases the scheme.
- The `APP_URL` alias and the `API_URL` override (and their `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variants) are only trimmed and stripped of trailing slashes.

Browsers always send `Origin` in canonical form: lowercase host, no default port, compressed IPv6. So a configured origin spelled any other way never matches:

| Configured value | In the trusted set | Browser sends |
|---|---|---|
| `ONECLI_EXTERNAL_URL=HTTPS://OneCLI.Example.com:443` | `https://OneCLI.Example.com:443` | `https://onecli.example.com` |
| `ONECLI_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://Extra.Example.com:80` | `http://Extra.Example.com:80` | `http://extra.example.com` |
| `ONECLI_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]:10254` | `http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]:10254` | `http://[::1]:10254` |
| `APP_URL=https://App.Example.com:443` | `https://App.Example.com:443` | `https://app.example.com` |

The loopback twin has the same problem: `ONECLI_EXTERNAL_URL=http://LOCALHOST:10254` gets no `127.0.0.1` twin, because the twin lookup compares the host exactly.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Set `ONECLI_EXTERNAL_URL=HTTPS://OneCLI.Example.com:443`, which is a valid spelling of `https://onecli.example.com`.
2. Call `trustedBrowserOrigin("https://onecli.example.com")`. It returns `undefined`, so the dashboard's own origin is treated as untrusted.
3. `buildTrustedOrigins(resolvePublicOrigins({ externalUrl: "HTTPS://OneCLI.Example.com:443" })).origins` is `["https://OneCLI.Example.com:443"]`.

From reading `cli-auth.ts`, a deployment with that setting would answer the dashboard's `POST /v1/auth/cli/confirm` with `403 Forbidden`, since that route compares the normalized `Origin` against this set.

### Expected behavior

A configured origin matches the browser's `Origin` however its scheme, host and default port are written. Trust should not widen: other hosts, schemes and ports stay untrusted.

I have a small fix with a regression test and will open a PR for it. I confirmed the behavior above with unit tests against the real module, not against a running deployment.

items.title: API client throws a TypeError instead of ApiError when an error body is JSON null
apiFetch mishandles Headers, tuple, and differently-cased header overrides
items.body:
### Description

`apiFetch` in `apps/web/src/lib/api-fetch.ts` accepts a standard `RequestInit`, so `options.headers` can be a `Headers` instance, an array of `[name, value]` pairs, or a plain object. It casts that value to `Record<string, string>` and spreads it after its own defaults:

```ts
headers: {
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
  ...(token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {}),
  ...(workspaceId ? { "X-Workspace-Id": workspaceId } : {}),
  ...(organizationId ? { "X-Organization-Id": organizationId } : {}),
  ...(options?.headers as Record<string, string> | undefined),
},
```

The cast changes nothing at runtime, so an override only takes effect when it's a plain object whose keys match the defaults' casing exactly:

- **A `Headers` instance** has no own enumerable properties, so the spread adds nothing and all of its headers are dropped.
- **An array of `[name, value]` pairs** spreads as index keys. `[["X-Workspace-Id", "ws-selected"]]` becomes a header named `0`, and the workspace derived from the URL is still sent.
- **A name that differs only in casing**, such as `{ "content-type": "text/plain" }`, ends up next to the default `Content-Type`, and the two values are joined into `application/json, text/plain`. On cloud, a lowercase `authorization` is joined onto the derived bearer token the same way.

Nothing is broken today. Every current caller that passes headers uses a plain object with the defaults' casing: `workspaceScope()` in `lib/api/client.ts`, the `X-Organization-Id` callers in `lib/api`, `lib/cli-auth/api.ts` and `credentials-flow.tsx`. The problem is latent. The first caller that uses one of the other forms the `RequestInit` type allows, or a lowercase name, silently sends the wrong headers.

### Steps to reproduce

In a Vitest test, stub `fetch` and put `window.location` on a workspace page (`/w/ws-from-url/agents`) so that `apiFetch` derives `X-Workspace-Id` from the URL. Read the headers `fetch` receives through `new Headers(init.headers)`, the way `fetch` itself reads them. Then:

1. Call `apiFetch("/v1/agents", { headers: new Headers({ "X-Workspace-Id": "ws-selected" }) })`. `get("x-workspace-id")` returns `ws-from-url`, not `ws-selected`.
2. Call it with `headers: [["X-Workspace-Id", "ws-selected"]]`. The result is the same, and there is also a header named `0`.
3. Call it with `headers: { "content-type": "text/plain" }`. `get("content-type")` returns `application/json, text/plain`.

### Expected behavior

Caller headers replace the defaults, whatever the `HeadersInit` form or the casing of the name. Nothing else about the request changes.

I have a small fix with a regression test and will open a PR for it.

items.title: Gateway wrongly requires credential for agent-browser page-text reads on never-before-seen hostnames
items.body:
**Summary**

A browser-automation tool (`agent-browser`, used from an agent container behind the OneCLI HTTPS gateway) can `open` and fully render a plain public webpage with no credential prompt, but a subsequent text-extraction step on that same already-open page fails with `credential_not_found`, even though the site needs no authentication at all.

**Repro**

1. `agent-browser open https://www.sportskeeda.com/mmo/how-easily-complete-missions-journey-ii-the-division-2-red-horizon-y8s3` — succeeds clean, no credential prompt, page renders.
2. `agent-browser get text body` on that same open page — returns, instead of page text:

```json
{"error":"credential_not_found","hostname":"www.sportskeeda.com",
 "message":"No credentials configured for www.sportskeeda.com in OneCLI...",
 "path":"/mmo/how-easily-complete-missions-journey-ii-the-division-2-red-horizon-y8s3",
 "secret_url":"https://<hive-instance>/w/<workspace>/connections/custom?create=generic&host=www%2Esportskeeda%2Ecom&path=%2F%2A"}
```

Confirmed reproducible on 5 distinct hostnames (sportskeeda.com, screwfix.com, wilko.com, homebase.co.uk, nufarm.com), across 3 separate agent containers/workspaces, 100% hit rate on retest. Common domains that had previously been fetched by these containers (google.com, bbc.co.uk, example.com) pass `get text` clean in the same test runs.

**Why this looks like a gateway bug, not intended behavior**

- `open` (full navigation) on the exact same URL never triggers a credential check.
- The credential gate is documented (gateway skill instructions) as being for actual API calls to connected services (Gmail, GitHub, Stripe, etc.) — not for reading arbitrary public webpages via a browser tool.
- None of the failing domains have any legitimate reason to need a stored credential for a page read, and the response actively invites creating a generic credential connection for them, which would be the wrong fix (masks the bug, grants an unnecessary credential).

**Working theory (unconfirmed — no gateway-internals access to verify further)**

`get text`'s extraction step may route through a lightweight HTTP fetch over the same proxied path used for real API calls, rather than reading Chromium's already-rendered DOM. If so, any *first-time-seen hostname* hitting that path gets treated like an unconnected API integration and gated, regardless of whether the destination needs auth. This would explain why previously-fetched common domains pass while every never-before-seen domain we tried failed identically — but this is a hypothesis based on external behavior only, not a confirmed root cause.

**Impact**

Any agent doing routine web reads via `agent-browser` behind the gateway is likely to trip this on the first new domain it visits, and could be tempted to click the provided credential-connection link to "fix" it — which would grant an unneeded credential rather than address the underlying gating bug.

Searched existing issues for `credential_not_found` and `browser credential` before filing; found none describing this specific interaction between `agent-browser`-style page reads and the credential gate.

items.title: Allow packaged deployments to supply provider options
items.body:
## Scope

The packaged control-plane composition point is `apps/web/src/lib/api/app.ts`, which is the sole caller of `createApiApp`. The Rust `onecli-gateway` is a separate data-plane process: it performs no control-plane principal resolution and writes no audit records, so it needs no equivalent hook. This proposal is therefore confined to the TypeScript control-plane API.

## Background

OneCLI already supports provider composition. `createApiApp(sessionProvider, options)` accepts `roleResolver`, `resourceHooks`, `connectionHooks`, `crypto`, `oauthOrg`, `appAvailability`, `strictApiKeyAuth` and others, registering each through the existing `init*` / `get*` provider functions. Editions use this today.

## Problem

That capability is available only to code that calls `createApiApp`. In a packaged deployment the application composes itself at `apps/web/src/lib/api/app.ts`, so an operator running the published image cannot supply provider implementations without patching the image.

Deployments that need a deployment-specific provider must therefore fork, even though the provider contract they need already exists and is stable.

## Part 1 — packaged composition

Let the packaged composition module optionally merge provider options supplied by the deployment — for example, by loading a module named in an environment variable and merging its exported options with the built-in ones.

Explicit non-goals: no plugin framework, no new lifecycle, no new provider concepts. This exposes an existing capability to a deployment context that currently cannot reach it. If no module is configured, behaviour is byte-identical to today.

## Part 2 — non-human principals

OneCLI currently models an authenticated API-key caller as a `User`: `ApiKey` carries `userId` and `userEmail`, `ensureApiKey` and `regenerateApiKey` key off `userId`, and `RoleResolver` is `getUserRole(userId, organizationId)`.

A deployment needing a service or machine caller must therefore either borrow a human credential, fabricate a `User` row, or use an organization-scoped bootstrap key. Each of these either misattributes the actor in audit or grants far more authority than the caller needs.

Proposed: a principal-shaped provider interface alongside `RoleResolver`, returning a small generic `PrincipalContext` of `principalId`, `principalType` and an opaque `authorizationContext`.

Upstream would own identity resolution and composition. Deployment-specific authorization models stay behind that seam and are explicitly **not** proposed for upstream.

## Part 3 — audit attribution

`AuditLog.userId` is currently `NOT NULL` with a required foreign key to `User`, so a non-human actor cannot be recorded without fabricating a user.

Proposed minimum: add a nullable `principalId` and an `actorType`; keep `userId` populated for human actors; allow it to be null for non-human actors.

`AuditLog` has one write site (`audit-service.ts`, `withAudit`) and no read sites, so this is a single chokepoint rather than a diffuse change.

## Backward compatibility

Human sessions and personal API keys are unchanged: `userId` stays populated for human actors, every new field is additive or a relaxation, and Part 1 is inert unless a deployment configures it.

Nothing in this proposal requires any deployment-specific package to be installed for existing behaviour to work.

## Motivating examples

An orchestrator process that provisions and configures agents needs to authenticate as itself, hold only the operations it actually calls, and appear in audit as a machine rather than as whichever engineer's key it borrowed.

The same shape applies to CI runners, schedulers, and other automation that acts on its own behalf rather than on behalf of a person.

---

Happy to discuss scope or shape before any code — raising this as an issue first per `CONTRIBUTING.md`. If the direction is acceptable, we're willing to contribute the implementation.

items.title: fix(runner): support Windows Docker Desktop named pipe for local dev on win32
items.body:
## Problem

Native Windows development with Docker Desktop fails when starting the OneCLI runner.

Running:

pnpm dev

starts the web, API, gateway and other services, but the runner crashes with:

Error: connect ENOENT /var/run/docker.sock

## Environment

- OS: Windows
- Docker Desktop: 29.6.2
- Node.js: 22.23.1
- pnpm: 9.0.0
- Docker context: desktop-linux

Docker itself is running correctly and `docker ps` works from PowerShell.

## Root cause

The runner defaults to:

/var/run/docker.sock

This is appropriate for Linux/POSIX environments, but native Windows Docker Desktop exposes the Docker Engine through the Windows named pipe:

//./pipe/docker_engine

The runner already supports the `RUNNER_DOCKER_SOCKET` environment variable, but when it is not set, native Windows development falls back to the Unix socket.

## Proposed solution

On `win32`, default the Docker socket to:

//./pipe/docker_engine

while preserving:

/var/run/docker.sock

for Linux/macOS and existing behavior when `RUNNER_DOCKER_SOCKET` is explicitly provided.

This would allow native Windows developers to run the local runner without manually configuring the Docker socket.

I would be happy to work on this if the maintainers agree with the approach.

items.title: Get Started page tells the CLI to use the gateway port, so `onecli auth login` fails
items.body:
## Steps to reproduce

1. Start OneCLI locally (`curl -fsSL https://onecli.sh/install | sh` or `docker compose`)
2. Open the dashboard and go to Install ("Get Started").
3. Copy the commands from step 2, "Install & sign in". They read:

   curl -fsSL onecli.sh/cli/install | sh
   onecli config set api-host http://localhost:10255
   onecli auth login --api-key oc_...

4. Run them.

**Result:** login fails with an error that says nothing about the cause.

```json
{
  "error": "could not verify API key: getting user: Bad Request",
  "code": "ERROR"
}
```

**Expected**: the copied commands work as-is.

## Solution

I managed to auth the CLI by specifying 10254 port instead of 10255:

```
onecli config set api-host http://localhost:10255
```

Apparently, the UI displays the wrong port.

## Environment

- OneCLI 1.45.0

## Agent investigation

### Why it happens 

  `API_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:10255`, the gateway port, in three places: `apps/web/src/lib/env.ts:27`,
  `packages/api/src/lib/env.ts:18`, and `apps/web/next.config.js:189` (when `API_DOMAIN` is unset). `.env.example:56` records the
  assumption behind it: `# OSS: localhost:10255 (gateway serves API too)`.

  `getInstallInfo()` passes it through as `apiUrl` (`apps/web/src/lib/actions/secrets.ts:80`) into the `config set api-host` line
  (`install-content.tsx:86`). The CLI verifies the key with `GET /user`, which on 10255 lands in the Axum `fallback()`
  (`apps/gateway/src/gateway.rs:698`) and comes back as a bodyless 400, so the CLI has nothing to report but "Bad Request".

  Two notes:

  - The published image is built without `API_DOMAIN`, so `localhost:10255` is baked into the bundle and operators can't override it
  at runtime. `apps/web/src/lib/env.ts` also doesn't read plain `API_URL`, unlike `packages/api/src/lib/env.ts`.
  - The `hint` in the working response resolves through `app-origin.ts` and is correct; `apiUrl` doesn't, so it's also wrong for any
  self-host reached over a LAN IP, proxy, or tunnel, not just for the port.

  ### Suggested fix

  Resolve `apiUrl` and `appUrl` in `getInstallInfo` as `configuredAppUrl() ?? originFromHeaders(await headers()) ?? APP_URL`, using
  `API_URL` only under `IS_CLOUD`.

  Then correct the `API_URL` defaults in both `env.ts` files and `next.config.js:189`, plus the `.env.example:56` comment.
  `GATEWAY_API_URL` / `GATEWAY_API_DOMAIN` stay as they are.

  Worth considering separately: giving `fallback()` a body that names the app port, since the gateway is the only component positioned
  to spot this misconfiguration.

items.title: Gateway upstream requests can remain pending indefinitely and require restart to recover
items.body:
## Summary

A running OneCLI gateway entered a state where HTTPS requests to GitHub through the credential-injecting MITM path stopped completing. Some clients completed the client-facing TLS handshake with OneCLI but received no HTTP response; Git/libcurl-GnuTLS sometimes failed earlier with a non-proper TLS termination.

Restarting OneCLI cleared the runtime state. After recovery, the same requests completed normally without changing Git's HTTP version, TLS version, certificate verification, proxy configuration, credential grant, or target repository.

The initiating cause of the stalled upstream state is unknown. An unhealthy pooled HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection or other stuck outbound state is plausible but not proven. The deterministic defect is that the gateway waits on upstream `reqwest` operations without a connection or response-header deadline and has no mechanism to rotate the shared client/pool after such a stall. A single bad upstream operation can therefore remain pending indefinitely and may require a process restart to recover.

## Impact

- Credential-injected HTTP/API traffic for an affected destination can stop completing.
- The client can receive a misleading secondary error such as a TLS handshake termination even when local CA trust and ordinary connectivity are valid.
- The gateway remains superficially healthy: its process and listener stay alive, and unrelated health/resource checks may remain normal.
- Recovery currently requires restarting the OneCLI container, interrupting all users of the gateway.

## Environment

- OneCLI image: `ghcr.io/onecli/onecli:1.45.0`
- Image digest: `sha256:d0177458b1f9ecece4abbe9abb6c5f925475357c1734f50a675d83a2ef9c8687`
- OneCLI source revision label: `84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a`
- Deployment: Docker, restart policy `unless-stopped`
- Host: Linux 6.8.0, x86_64
- Git: 2.43.0 (`1:2.43.0-1ubuntu7.3`)
- Git HTTP transport: libcurl-GnuTLS
  - `libcurl3t64-gnutls=8.5.0-2ubuntu10.11`
  - `libgnutls30t64=3.8.3-1.1ubuntu3.6`
- curl control client: curl/libcurl 8.5.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13 and nghttp2 1.59.0
- Proxy listener: standard local OneCLI gateway port 10255
- Target observed in the field: public GitHub smart-HTTP endpoint for a public repository
- A GitHub credential connection was available to the agent and the MITM path applied one injection in a later sanitized cold-gateway control.

No credential value, proxy authorization value, agent/project identifier, request header, CA key, or private endpoint is included here.

## Chronology

The exact same OneCLI 1.45.0 image successfully served Hermes Agent update fetches on:

- 2026-08-03
- 2026-08-04
- 2026-08-05
- 2026-08-07
- 2026-08-09
- 2026-08-10
- 2026-08-14 (two successful update runs)

On 2026-08-16, three update attempts failed with:

```text
fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent.git/':
gnutls_handshake() failed: The TLS connection was non-properly terminated.
```

This makes the problem intermittent. The image was not inherently unable to serve Git traffic after deployment.

## Field reproduction

The affected operation was an ordinary Git fetch through the configured OneCLI proxy:

```bash
timeout 60 git -C <public-repository-checkout> fetch origin main
```

Observed results during the incident:

- ordinary fetch hung until the external timeout or failed with the GnuTLS error above;
- CONNECT to the local OneCLI proxy returned `200`;
- forcing the Git client-facing leg to HTTP/1.1 was not a reliable fix: it succeeded in one early control but later HTTP/1.1 probes also stalled;
- disabling TLS verification was never attempted and is not needed;
- no repository-local or global Git HTTP/TLS override was present after recovery.

A neutral public reproduction target can use:

```bash
git ls-remote https://github.com/onecli/onecli.git HEAD
```

The original stuck runtime state was cleared by restart, so the exact field failure is no longer continuously reproducible.

## Protocol observations during the stuck state

A redacted probe recorded protocol milestones only; it did not retain or print request headers or credentials.

### Git/libcurl-GnuTLS

For both requested TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 client configurations:

- proxy CONNECT returned `200`;
- no certificate/negotiated-TLS milestone was observed;
- the operation remained pending for approximately 17 seconds until the probe's external timeout.

### curl/OpenSSL

For both TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, using HTTP/1.1 on the client-facing leg:

- proxy CONNECT returned `200`;
- ClientHello and ServerHello were observed;
- the OneCLI-issued certificate was received;
- the requested TLS version was negotiated;
- ALPN selected HTTP/1.1;
- no HTTP response arrived within 15 seconds.

The curl results place at least one failure after a successful client-facing TLS handshake. The GnuTLS error is therefore not sufficient evidence that CA trust, TLS 1.3, or the client-facing protocol was the primary cause.

An early local harness label called these curl cases `tls_handshake_timeout`; that label was corrected after reviewing the milestones. The issue intentionally reports the milestones rather than the stale label.

## Recovery observations

After OneCLI was restarted and startup had settled:

- curl TLS 1.2 + HTTP/1.1: success in about 0.28 seconds;
- curl TLS 1.3 + HTTP/1.1: success in about 0.28 seconds;
- Git through HTTP/1.1: success in about 0.9 seconds;
- Git with HTTP/2 on the client-facing Git-to-OneCLI leg: success in about 0.9 seconds;
- ordinary Git fetches worked without HTTP/TLS overrides.

A second controlled restart reached three consecutive successful checks for all of the following within approximately five seconds of container restart:

- OneCLI web health;
- neutral public HTTPS through the proxy;
- GitHub API through the proxy;
- GitHub smart-HTTP path through the proxy.

The restart removed pending tasks and rebuilt the shared `reqwest` connection pool. This supports an in-memory/runtime-state failure but does not uniquely identify the initiating fault.

## Other controls

- Basic public HTTPS through OneCLI worked after recovery.
- GitHub API, plain HTTP, and an existing internal credential-injection lane worked after recovery.
- A cold isolated gateway process performed the expected GitHub MITM path:
  - cache miss and database resolution;
  - one deferred connection;
  - successful client TLS handshake;
  - successful upstream TCP/TLS connection;
  - one injection applied;
  - HTTP response returned and the upstream connection was pooled.
- The container did not show CPU, PID, file-descriptor, or obvious memory exhaustion during diagnosis.
- Host Git, libcurl-GnuTLS, and GnuTLS packages were already at the latest versions available from the configured Ubuntu repositories.
- Direct no-proxy Git controls were inconclusive because this host may require the gateway for outbound access.

## Version/regression analysis

This does not appear to be a deterministic OneCLI 1.45.0 regression:

- the same image served successful Git updates through 2026-08-14;
- OneCLI v1.41.0 and v1.45.0 use the same relevant HTTP stack versions:
  - reqwest 0.12.28
  - hyper 1.8.1
  - rustls 0.23.37
  - Tokio 1.50.0
- the unbounded forwarding wait is present in both versions.

The client-facing Git leg did negotiate HTTP/2 in one recovered control, but Cargo feature inspection shows that OneCLI's upstream `reqwest` client is built without reqwest's `http2` feature. The upstream client pool is therefore HTTP/1.1. This rules out a pooled upstream HTTP/2 connection as the mechanism in this build. It does not identify the initiating cause; an unhealthy HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection, a stuck request, or another transient outbound state remains plausible.

## Deterministic source-level reproduction

The gateway's normal forwarding path awaits the upstream request without a gateway-level bound:

```rust
let upstream_resp = upstream
    .send()
    .await
    .with_context(|| format!("forwarding to {url}"))?;
```

A focused test used a local upstream that:

1. accepted the TCP connection;
2. accepted the request;
3. never returned HTTP response headers.

Against the existing behavior, OneCLI did not terminate the operation itself. Only the test's outer 250 ms guard stopped it. A prototype helper with a supplied 50 ms response-header bound made the same focused test pass.

This proves the missing containment independently of the unknown field trigger.

## Expected behavior

When an upstream operation stops making progress, the gateway should:

1. terminate the wait after a configurable, documented bound;
2. return a sanitized and accurate gateway timeout response;
3. ensure future requests do not continue leasing the same suspect client/pool generation;
4. avoid automatically replaying requests, especially non-idempotent or streaming requests;
5. preserve long-lived response streaming after response headers have arrived;
6. preserve existing TLS-verification policy, including separation of normal and explicitly configured skip-verification clients.

## Proposed direction for discussion

This is intentionally a proposal, not a requirement for a particular implementation.

One possible implementation is:

- configure a bounded upstream connect timeout;
- bound only the wait for response headers (`RequestBuilder::send()`), not the streamed response body;
- on a response-header timeout, return a sanitized HTTP 504 such as `upstream_timeout`;
- rotate the affected shared `reqwest::Client` generation so subsequent requests lease a fresh pool;
- do not automatically retry/replay the failed request;
- make concurrent timeouts against one generation perform at most one rotation;
- keep normal-verification and skip-verification client generations independent.

Maintainers may prefer a different implementation. The core request is bounded failure plus automatic escape from suspect pooled state, without weakening TLS or replaying requests.

## Suggested regression coverage

- silent upstream accepts TCP/request but never sends headers: bounded timeout;
- timeout maps to sanitized HTTP 504 `upstream_timeout`;
- future request uses a fresh client generation and succeeds;
- concurrent timeouts rotate one generation once;
- normal-verification and skip-verification pools remain independent;
- headers arrive before the bound but the body streams longer: stream succeeds;
- no automatic replay, including POST;
- existing redirect, TLS, credential-injection, and streaming tests remain green.

## Related but distinct reports

- #424 concerns AAAA SERVFAIL/timeout handling and IPv4 fallback.
- #251 concerned Git credential injection on `github.com` and was fixed separately.
- PR #259 concerned absolute-form HTTPS routing and later documented a wrong-port axios case.

None of those appears to track an indefinitely pending upstream request plus client-pool recovery.

items.title: OpenAI API-key injection breaks fresh Codex OAuth login with invalid_client
items.body:
## Summary

When an `openai` secret in API-key mode is stored for `api.openai.com`, OneCLI 1.45.0 also applies it to `auth.openai.com` and injects it as an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header.

That added header causes a fresh Codex ChatGPT OAuth authorization-code exchange at `https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token` to fail with:

```text
401 Unauthorized
invalid_client: Invalid client specified.
```

This prevents `codex login` from completing whenever Codex traffic is routed through the authenticated OneCLI gateway. It also sends the API key to an OpenAI-owned hostname outside the secret's configured `hostPattern`.

## Environment

- OneCLI server: `1.45.0`
- Current `main`: `84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a`
- Codex CLI: `0.147.0`
- OneCLI secret: type `openai`, API-key mode, `hostPattern=api.openai.com`
- Client: WSL Ubuntu, with HTTPS routed through the authenticated OneCLI proxy

## Steps to reproduce

1. Store an OpenAI API-key secret in OneCLI with type `openai` and `hostPattern=api.openai.com`.
2. Grant it to the agent used by an authenticated OneCLI proxy connection.
3. Route Codex HTTPS traffic through that proxy.
4. Start from logged-out Codex state and run `codex login`.
5. Complete the browser authorization flow.

The browser returns to Codex, but the token exchange fails with `token_exchange_failed` / `invalid_client`.

## Controlled evidence

I sent the same synthetic, already-expired authorization-code form to the token endpoint in three conditions; no live authorization code or credential was used in this control:

| Request path | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Direct to `auth.openai.com` | `401 token_expired` |
| Through the OneCLI gateway | `401 invalid_client` |
| Direct, with a synthetic `Authorization: Bearer not-a-real-key` header | The same `401 invalid_client` response as the gateway path |

The OneCLI gateway logged the proxied token request with `injections_applied=1`.

The direct request proves that the public Codex client ID and form shape reach the intended token-validation path. Adding only the Authorization header reproduces the gateway failure exactly.

## Cause

`secret_host_patterns` expands every `openai` secret to `*.openai.com`, regardless of whether it contains an API key or a ChatGPT OAuth credential:

https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/secret_inject.rs#L162-L187

API-key mode then injects the secret as an Authorization bearer value:

https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/secret_inject.rs#L43-L86

This also contradicts the default-interception contract, which says real Codex login requests are forwarded to `auth.openai.com` untouched:

https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/default_interceptions.rs#L84-L89

The broad OpenAI host expansion was introduced in commit `1633c21` / PR #438.

## Expected behavior

- An API-key-mode secret configured for `api.openai.com` should not be injected into `auth.openai.com` OAuth requests or ChatGPT subscription endpoints.
- A real Codex authorization-code exchange should be forwarded without an API-key Authorization header.
- ChatGPT OAuth-mode secrets can retain their separate ChatGPT host coverage.
- The existing synthetic handling for the `onecli-managed` refresh placeholder should continue to work.

One possible fix is to make extra OpenAI host patterns depend on `metadata.authMode`, rather than only `secret_type`, and to ensure that a real `/oauth/token` request which is not synthetically intercepted bypasses secret injection.

## Workaround

Bypass OneCLI for the subscription authentication and ChatGPT hosts while keeping `api.openai.com` proxied:

```text
NO_PROXY=auth.openai.com,chatgpt.com,.chatgpt.com
```

## Related issues

- #433 concerns refreshing a vaulted ChatGPT OAuth credential and is not this failure.
- #425 concerns Codex model-backend routing after OneCLI-managed login and is not this failure.

items.title: Generic secret hostPattern accepts ports but gateway strips them before matching
items.body:
## Summary

Generic secrets can be created with a port-qualified `hostPattern`, such as
`example.internal:3000`, but the gateway strips the request port before resolving
secrets. The stored pattern therefore never matches.

This prevents distinct credentials from being assigned to services hosted on
different ports of the same hostname—a common pattern for local and self-hosted MCP
servers.

## Reproduction

1. Create a generic secret with:

   - `hostPattern`: `example.internal:3000`
   - `pathPattern`: `/api/mcp`
   - injection: `Authorization: Bearer {value}`

2. Attach the secret to an agent.
3. Send an HTTP request through the authenticated OneCLI proxy:

   ```text
   POST http://example.internal:3000/api/mcp
   ```

4. The gateway forwards the request without injecting the secret.

Observed gateway output:

```text
HTTP_PROXY scheme=http injection_count=0 policy_count=0
credential not found ... status=401
```

The agent was confirmed to have access to the secret.

## Cause

Both proxy paths remove the port before credential resolution:

- CONNECT handler:
  https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/gateway.rs#L777-L793
- Plain HTTP handler:
  https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/gateway.rs#L947-L965

`connect::resolve` then caches and resolves exclusively by hostname:

https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/connect.rs#L1540-L1600

The matcher performs an exact or wildcard comparison against that stripped hostname:

https://github.com/onecli/onecli/blob/84ccaf74ce6350f8925675457b48272c29f32c1a/apps/gateway/src/connect.rs#L1745-L1772

The API validation rejects URLs and paths but does not reject an exact
`hostname:port` pattern, so the configuration is accepted but cannot work at runtime.

## Why removing the port is not always safe

A hostname-only workaround is unsafe when separate services on different ports use
different credentials.

For example:

```text
example.internal:3000 → credential A
example.internal:3200 → credential B
```

If both secrets are changed to `example.internal` and have overlapping paths, both
can match the same request and attempt to set `Authorization`. The selected value
becomes order-dependent and could send a credential to the wrong service.

## Proposed semantics

Would the project accept port-qualified host patterns with these semantics?

- `example.internal` continues matching the hostname on any port.
- `example.internal:3000` matches only port 3000.
- Wildcard behavior remains backward compatible.
- Credential-resolution cache keys include the normalized effective port so rules
  cannot leak across ports.
- HTTP proxy and CONNECT/MITM paths use the same endpoint matching.
- Secret policy targets use the same endpoint semantics as injection.
- Validation accepts supported `hostname:port` forms and rejects malformed ones.

Provider detection and TLS certificate generation should continue using the bare
hostname.

## Versions

- Reproduced on OneCLI server `1.38.0`
- Current upstream `main` at `84ccaf7` / release `1.45.0` still contains the same
  hostname-only resolution path

items.body:
the gateway's cors layer uses `alloworigin::mirror_request()` together with `allow_credentials(true)` (apps/gateway/src/gateway.rs), so it reflects whatever origin the request carries. in local mode — the default quick-start setup with no `nextauth_secret` — the auth extractor resolves the `local-admin` user without reading any request state. together, any website a user visits can make credentialed calls to the gateway api and read the responses.

verified in a real browser (chromium) from a different origin, with `credentials: "include"` and no tokens:

- `get /v1/approvals/pending` returned the victim's pending human-approval request (agent identity, host, path, headers, body summary)
- `post /v1/approvals/{id}/decision {"decision":"approve"}` approved it, and the gateway released the agent's gated request upstream

the same reach applies to `/me`, `/v1/vault/{provider}/status` and `/pair`, the 1password picker, and `/v1/cache/invalidate`. binding to 127.0.0.1 does not help — the attacker's javascript runs in the victim's browser.

items.title: Gateway can never refresh vaulted ChatGPT (Codex) OAuth tokens: refresh request omits client_id
items.body:
## Summary

The gateway's automatic OpenAI OAuth refresh (`refresh_openai_oauth_if_expired` in `apps/gateway/src/secret_inject.rs`) always fails, because the refresh request to `https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token` sends only `grant_type` and `refresh_token`. The endpoint requires `client_id` and rejects the request with 400:

```
WARN onecli_gateway::secret_inject: openai oauth token refresh failed, using expired token error=openai oauth token refresh failed (400 Bad Request): {
  "error": {
    "message": "Missing 'client_id'",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "param": "client_id",
    "code": "missing_required_parameter"
  }
```

The gateway then falls back to injecting the expired token, so every request to `chatgpt.com` gets 401:

```
WARN ... onecli_gateway::gateway::websocket: WebSocket: upstream rejected upgrade host=chatgpt.com:443 status=401
```

Net effect: a vaulted ChatGPT-subscription session (e.g. for driving the Codex CLI through the gateway) hard-expires roughly every 10 days and requires a full interactive re-login, despite the docs saying "The gateway automatically refreshes the access token when it expires using the stored refresh token — no manual re-authentication needed."

Downstream symptom worth noting for searchability: Codex CLI reacts to the 401 by attempting to rewrite its own `~/.codex/auth.json`, which is the gateway's read-only sentinel stub, so end users see `Reconnecting... 2/5: Read-only file system (os error 30)`.

## Reproduce

1. Vault a ChatGPT-subscription `auth.json` (`onecli secrets create --file ... --host-pattern chatgpt.com`), use it through the gateway.
2. Wait for the access token to expire (~10 days).
3. Observe the 400/401 pairs above in gateway logs; all Codex traffic fails until manual re-auth.

## Fix

Include the Codex CLI's public OAuth `client_id` (`app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann`, hardcoded in the open-source Codex CLI, e.g. `codex-rs/login/src/auth/manager.rs`) in the refresh form — it identifies the app that issued the vaulted session and is not a secret. One-line change; PR follows.

Verified against `main` as of 2026-07-19 (`apps/gateway/src/secret_inject.rs`, `refresh_openai_oauth_token`).

items.title: Gateway: API-key secret injection preempts OAuth app injection on shared hosts (www.googleapis.com)
items.body:
## Summary

When a host carries **both** a vaulted API-key secret and one or more OAuth **app** connections, the gateway injects only the secret and **skips OAuth app resolution entirely** for that host. OAuth requests then reach the provider with no `Authorization` header and fail upstream with `401`, which the gateway surfaces as `app_not_connected`.

This breaks **every** Google Workspace OAuth app (Calendar, Drive, and the Gmail legacy path) for any project that also has a **YouTube Data API key** vaulted — because all of them live on `www.googleapis.com`. Requests to the providers' **dedicated** hosts (`gmail.googleapis.com`, `tasks.googleapis.com`) are unaffected, which is the tell.

This is distinct from #236/#237 (which added missing `/batch/` path rules): here the path rules are correct and present, but app resolution never runs because a secret is bound to the same host.

## Repro

In a project that has (a) a Google Calendar OAuth app connected **and** (b) a YouTube Data API key vaulted as a secret on `www.googleapis.com` (path `/youtube/`, query param `key`):

```bash
# Agent request through the gateway, no auth header — gateway should inject the Bearer:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  "https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3/users/me/calendarList"
# => 401   (gateway logs: "app not connected ... provider=google-calendar")

# Same OAuth connection, dedicated host — works:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  "https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/profile"
# => 200
```

Remove the YouTube key (or query the provider before the key is vaulted) and the calendar request returns `200`. So it is the *coexistence* of a secret and an app on the same host that triggers it — the OAuth token itself is valid (it works on the dedicated host).

## Root cause

App-connection resolution is gated on there being **no** secret rules. In `apps/gateway/src/gateway/mitm.rs`:

```rust
let mut injection_rules = resp.injection_rules; // from secrets
// If no secret rules, try app connections (per-request disambiguation)
if injection_rules.is_empty() && !resp.app_connections.is_empty() {
    // ... resolve_app_injection_for_request ...
    injection_rules = rules;   // and: replace, not merge
}
```

The YouTube key makes `injection_rules` non-empty, so the whole block is skipped and `resolve_app_injection_for_request` is never called. The identical pattern is in `apps/gateway/src/gateway.rs` (the HTTP-proxy path).

Secret rules and app rules are both **path-scoped** `InjectionRule`s (`/youtube/*` for the key vs `/calendar/*` for the OAuth Bearer), so they can and should coexist rather than one preempting the other.

## Evidence

Instrumenting the `apply_injections` call site, a calendar request carries only the youtube rule:

```
path=/calendar/v3/... n_rules=1 patterns=[("/youtube/*", 1)] injection_count=0 auth_len=0
```

After the fix (run app resolution regardless and merge), the same request carries both, and the `/calendar/*` Bearer applies:

```
path=/calendar/v3/... n_rules=3 patterns=[("/youtube/*",1),("/calendar/*",1),("/batch/calendar/*",1)] injection_count=1 auth_len=260
```

A `/youtube/*` request still injects the key and correctly ignores the non-matching OAuth rules.

## Proposed fix

Run app resolution whenever app connections exist, and **merge** the resulting rules with any secret rules (`injection_rules.extend(rules)`) instead of gating on `injection_rules.is_empty()` and replacing. Apply to both `mitm.rs` and `gateway.rs`. Reproduced against `main` (32b5852).

Happy to open a PR with the fix + a regression test (I have both ready) if the direction looks right.

## Environment

- OneCLI `main` (32b5852); also reproduced on the released `latest` image.
- Self-hosted, Google BYOC OAuth apps (Gmail/Calendar/Tasks/Drive) + YouTube Data API key as a vaulted secret.

Related: #236 / #237 (batch path rules — different root cause), #307 (token endpoint routing — adjacent).

---

*Disclosure: I found this bug while integrating OneCLI, diagnosed it with an AI coding assistant, and verified the repro, root cause, and fix against a local build myself before filing.*

items.body:
## Description

When an agent uses the **Codex** provider with a **ChatGPT-OAuth** (subscription) credential, every model call fails with:

```
401 Unauthorized: WebSocket upgrade rejected by upstream (wss://api.openai.com/v1/responses)
```

## Root cause

OneCLI serves codex a stub `id_token` from `packages/api/src/lib/codex-stubs.ts`. Its payload advertises a **free** plan:

```json
"https://api.openai.com/auth": { "chatgpt_plan_type": "free", ... }
```

codex-cli (>= 0.14x) selects its model backend from this claim:

- `free` → `wss://api.openai.com/v1/responses` (API mode). OneCLI injects the ChatGPT-OAuth **subscription** token here, which `api.openai.com` does not accept → **401**.
- a paid plan → `wss://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`, where the injected subscription token **is** valid → 200.

So the credential injection itself is correct — the stub just steers codex to the wrong (API-key) endpoint.

## Evidence (gateway logs, one Codex session)

```
forward    GET  chatgpt.com/backend-api/...             status=200  injections_applied=2
websocket       api.openai.com/v1/responses (upgrade)   status=401  upstream rejected upgrade
```

HTTP calls to `chatgpt.com` inject fine; only the `api.openai.com` WS upgrade 401s — consistent with wrong-endpoint routing, not a missing injection.

## Fix

Advertise a paid plan in the stub `id_token` so codex routes to the `chatgpt.com` backend. The real entitlement stays enforced upstream by the injected token; this claim only steers routing. PR to follow.

## Environment

- OneCLI `1.41.0`
- codex-cli `>= 0.14x`, ChatGPT-OAuth (subscription) credential

items.title: Gateway returns 502 ("resolution_failed") when a host's AAAA record SERVFAILs, instead of falling back to IPv4

labels.name: area/gateway
labels.description: Proxy, routing, TLS, DNS, credential injection

labels.name: has-pr
labels.description: A community PR exists for this issue

items.body:
## Summary

The gateway fails a request whenever the destination host's **AAAA (IPv6) record lookup returns SERVFAIL or times out**, even though the host has a perfectly valid A record and is reachable over IPv4. Instead of falling back to the A record (as `curl` and every browser do — RFC 8305 "Happy Eyeballs"), the gateway's HTTP client treats the failed AAAA leg as fatal and returns a generic 502:

```json
{"error":"resolution_failed","message":"OneCLI gateway failed to resolve rules for this request."}
```

The user-facing message is also misleading — it implies a **policy/rule** resolution failure, but the underlying cause is DNS/connection forwarding. This sent us on a long debugging detour (we assumed a rule/blocklist/credential mapping problem before finding the real cause in the gateway logs).

## Environment

- Gateway image: `ghcr.io/onecli/onecli:1.36.0`
- CLI: `onecli 2.2.5`
- Host: Linux, rootless Docker, container on a user-defined bridge network (`127.0.0.11` embedded DNS → host resolver). Gateway container has **no global IPv6 address**.

## Reproduction

Any host whose authoritative nameservers **SERVFAIL / time out on AAAA** while answering A correctly triggers it. A real public example at time of writing is `yashir-agent.555.co.il` (authoritative NS: `dns.netvision.net.il`, `nypop.netvision.net.il`):

```bash
# A record: clean
$ dig +short yashir-agent.555.co.il A
194.90.184.238

# AAAA: SERVFAIL / timeout (broken upstream, but a well-behaved client should ignore this)
$ dig yashir-agent.555.co.il AAAA
;; ->>HEADER<<- ... status: SERVFAIL
# or: ;; communications error to <resolver>#53: timed out

# Through the OneCLI gateway → 502
$ curl -x http://x:<agent-token>@127.0.0.1:10255 https://yashir-agent.555.co.il/
{"error":"resolution_failed","message":"OneCLI gateway failed to resolve rules for this request."}

# Same host, same Docker network, plain curl (glibc AND musl) → 200,
# because curl falls back to the A record after the AAAA lookup fails
$ docker run --rm --network <gateway-net> alpine sh -c \
    'apk add -q curl && curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} connect=%{time_connect}s\n" https://yashir-agent.555.co.il/'
200 connect=2.0s      # the ~2s is the AAAA timeout before the A fallback
```

## Gateway logs (the real cause, vs the client-facing message)

```
WARN session{host=yashir-agent.555.co.il:443 agent=...}: onecli_gateway::gateway::mitm:
     request forwarding failed host=yashir-agent.555.co.il:443
     error=forwarding to https://yashir-agent.555.co.il:443/...
    0: error sending request for url (https://yashir-agent.555.co.il/...)
    1: client error (Connect)
    2: dns error
```

Note this is distinct from a genuine NXDOMAIN, which additionally logs `3: failed to lookup address information: Name does not resolve`. Here the A record resolves fine — only the AAAA leg fails, and that alone kills the request.

## Expected behavior

Match `curl`/browser behavior (RFC 8305): if the AAAA lookup fails/SERVFAILs/times out but the A lookup succeeds, connect over IPv4. A broken *upstream* AAAA record should never make an IPv4-reachable host unreachable through the gateway — especially in a container with no IPv6 connectivity at all.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Resolver robustness:** when resolving for the upstream connection, don't treat a failed AAAA leg as fatal if the A leg succeeded (implement Happy Eyeballs, or at minimum fall back to A-only). If the reqwest/hyper client is used with a custom resolver (e.g. hickory-dns), configure it to tolerate partial (single-family) failures; or gate AAAA on `AI_ADDRCONFIG`-style local-IPv6 detection so a container with no IPv6 doesn't query/require AAAA at all.
2. **Error clarity:** the client-facing 502 says "failed to resolve **rules**," but the actual failure is DNS/upstream forwarding. Surface a message that reflects the real cause (e.g. `upstream_dns_error` vs `policy_resolution_error`) so operators don't chase a non-existent rule/policy problem.

## Impact

Any agent behind the gateway silently loses access to otherwise-healthy hosts that happen to have a broken/slow IPv6 record — a surprisingly common real-world DNS misconfiguration. The failure is opaque (looks like a policy error) and there's no gateway-side config knob to force IPv4 or tolerate the AAAA failure.

items.body:
Hi maintainers 👋

**Feature request:** Add xAI / Grok as an OAuth app connector, so users can connect their xAI account through OneCLI and have the gateway inject refreshed xAI OAuth credentials for requests to `api.x.ai`.

**Motivation:** OneCLI supports OAuth connectors for GitHub/Google/Gmail/Resend and API-key secrets, but there's no first-class xAI/Grok connector. With Grok increasingly used by CLI/agent tooling, a native vault-injected, auto-refreshing connector would be valuable.

**Status:** I have a complete, working, tested implementation ready — happy to open the PR as soon as there's agreement on the design questions below.

**How it's currently implemented:**
- **TS/API** (`packages/api/src/apps/xai.ts` + `types.ts`, `routes/apps.ts`, `apps/registry.ts`, `app-permissions/xai.ts`, provider icon): registers the `xai` connector (host `api.x.ai`, `Authorization: Bearer {value}` injection).
- **Two OAuth flows:**
  - *Authorization-code + PKCE* (`S256`) through the existing `/v1/apps/:provider/authorize` → `/callback` dashboard UX (added a `pkce` flag to `ConnectionMethod` + a server-held verifier cookie).
  - *RFC 8628 device-code* via new `POST /v1/apps/xai/device-code` (start) + `/device-code/exchange` (poll) — agent/CLI-friendly.
- **Rust gateway** (`apps/gateway/src/apps.rs`, `connect.rs`): provider registration + **public-client refresh** (form-encoded `client_id` + `refresh_token`, *no* `client_secret`, since xAI is a public OIDC client).
- xAI OIDC endpoints: `auth.x.ai/oauth2/{authorize,device/code,token,userinfo,revoke}`; discovery confirms `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, device-code, `none` auth method, and PKCE `S256`.

**Verification (all green):**
- `pnpm check` (typecheck) + `pnpm build` pass.
- Tests: **283 API (Vitest) + 470 Rust gateway unit + 8 integration** pass; added mocked tests for authorize, token exchange, device-code start/poll/exchange, and gateway public-client refresh.
- **End-to-end verified locally:** device-code login with a real xAI account → token stored in the vault → a real `grok-4.3` chat call routed through the gateway returned a correct response using the injected OAuth Bearer.
- Branch is squashed to a single Conventional Commit; no CLA/DCO required per the repo.

**Design questions before I open the PR:**
1. **Client ID:** xAI exposes a public OAuth client for its official grok CLI. Prefer the connector to default to that public client id (overridable via config / `XAI_CLIENT_ID`), like several CLI OAuth integrations reuse public clients — or require users to bring their own?
2. **Flows:** ship both auth-code+PKCE and device-code, or just the dashboard PKCE flow?

**Note:** grok model region-availability (some models are restricted by region) is a runtime/inference concern for callers, not a connector concern — the connector only handles OAuth, refresh, and gateway injection.

Thanks! Happy to open the PR immediately on a thumbs-up.

items.title: OAuth callback always redirects to localhost:10254 when APP_URL is not set (the fallback never runs)
items.body:
## What happens

When someone self-hosts OneCLI and does not set the `APP_URL` variable, every OAuth connect flow ends on the wrong page. The provider consent step works. But the last redirect sends the browser to `http://localhost:10254` instead of the real site.

## Why it happens

In `packages/api/src/routes/apps.ts`, the callback picks the redirect target like this:

```ts
const appOrigin = APP_URL || apiOrigin;
```

It looks like it will fall back to the request origin (`apiOrigin`) when `APP_URL` is empty. But `APP_URL` here is the constant from `env.ts`:

```ts
process.env.APP_URL ?? process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "http://localhost:10254"
```

This constant always has a value. It is never empty. So the `|| apiOrigin` part never runs. It is dead code. When `APP_URL` is not set, `appOrigin` is always `http://localhost:10254`.

The first half of the flow already does this right. The consent `redirect_uri` comes from the request (`lib/request-origin.ts`, added in #325). So the flow half works: consent is fine, then the last hop strands the user on localhost.

## How to see it

1. Self-host the gateway on any host that is not localhost. Do not set `APP_URL`.
2. Connect any OAuth provider from the dashboard.
3. Consent works. Then the browser lands on `http://localhost:10254/app-connect/...`

I saw this live on a headless install of v1.40.0 (`61f6238`). The same code is on main today (`fe0981f`, checked 2026-07-08, `apps.ts` line 435).

## Suggested fix (about 2 lines)

In the callback, read the raw env values the same way `lib/request-origin.ts` does:

```ts
process.env.APP_URL ?? process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL
```

This is `undefined` when not set. Then the existing `|| apiOrigin` fallback starts working. The newer request-origin code (after #407) already uses this raw-env pattern, so the fix matches what the project already does.

## Related, but not blocking

The links agents hand out (`lib/skills/gateway-skill.ts` through `lib/dashboard-url.ts`) use the same constant, so they have the same localhost default. There is no request in scope there, so that one needs its own design call. I mention it here so it is not forgotten.

---
